questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the holy scriptures?
questions.reference_answer: The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving Knowledge, Faith and Obedience; Although the light of Nature, and the works of Creation and Providence do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom and power of God, as to leave men unexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God and His will, which is necessary unto Salvation. Therefore it pleased the Lord at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that His will unto his Church; and afterward for the better preserving, and propagating of the Truth, and for the more sure Establishment, and Comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan, and of the World, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the Holy Scriptures to be most necessary, those former ways of Gods revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the Name of Holy Scripture or the Word of God written; are now contained all the Books of the Old and New Testament which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Of the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, The Acts of the Apostles, Pauls Epistle to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Phillippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the First and Second Epistles of Peter, the First, Second and Third Epistles of John, the Epistle of Jude, the Revelation. The Books commonly called Apocrypha not being of Divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon (or rule) of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority to the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved or made use of, then other humane writings. The Authority of the Holy Scripture for which it ought to be believed dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or Church; but wholly upon God (who is truth it self) the Author thereof; therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church of God, to an high and reverent esteem of the Holy Scriptures; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the Doctrine, and the Majesty of the stile, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God) the full discovery it makes of the only way of mans salvation, and many other incomparable Excellencies, and intire perfections thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence it self to be the Word of God; yet notwithstanding; our full perswasion, and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our Hearts. The whole Councel of God concerning all things necessary for his own Glory, Mans Salvation, Faith and Life, is either expressely set down or necessarily contained in the Holy Scripture; unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new Revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God, to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word, and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church common to humane actions and societies; which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation, are so clearly propounded, and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew, (which was the Native language of the people of God of old) and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the Nations being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and Providence kept pure in all Ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of Religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God, who have a right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded in the fear of God to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every Nation, unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and through patience and comfort of the Scriptures may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture it self: And therefore when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold but one) it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. The supream judge by which all controversies of Religion are to be determined, and all Decrees of Councels, opinions of antient Writers, Doctrines of men, and private Spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit, into which Scripture so delivered, our faith is finally resolved.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the Second London Baptist Confession) dedicates its **first chapter** entirely to the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures.

Because the 1689 Confession is a Reformed (Calvinistic) Baptist document, its teaching on Scripture is heavily influenced by the **Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)** and the **Savoy Declaration (1658)**. It presents a "high view" of the Bible, emphasizing its divine origin, authority, and sufficiency.

Here is a summary of what the 1689 Confession teaches about the Holy Scriptures, broken down by its key theological points:

### 1. Divine Inspiration and Authority (Chapter 1, Sections 1–3)
*   **God-Breathed:** The Confession teaches that the Holy Scriptures are the "Word of God written." They were written by holy men of God who were moved by the Holy Spirit.
*   **Supreme Authority:** The authority of Scripture depends entirely on God (who is truth itself), not on the testimony of the Church or any human authority. Therefore, it is to be received and believed because it is the Word of God.
*   **Binding Conscience:** Because it is God's Word, it binds the conscience of believers. It is the "infallible rule of faith and obedience."

### 2. The Canon of Scripture (Chapter 1, Sections 2 & 3)
*   **The Books:** It affirms the standard 66 books of the Protestant canon (39 Old Testament, 27 New Testament).
*   **The Apocrypha:** It explicitly rejects the Apocrypha (books found in the Catholic Old Testament but not the Hebrew canon). It states these books are not of divine inspiration, are not part of the canon, and therefore have no authority in the Church of God.
*   **Closed Canon:** The Confession teaches that the canon is closed. No new revelations or traditions are to be added to the Scripture.

### 3. The Necessity of Scripture (Chapter 1, Section 5)
*   While God's works of creation and providence show His power and deity, they are **not sufficient** to reveal the knowledge of God and His will necessary for salvation.
*   Therefore, the written Word is necessary for the church and for individuals to know the way of salvation.

### 4. The Clarity (Perspicuity) of Scripture (Chapter 1, Section 7)
*   **Not All Equally Clear:** The Confession acknowledges that not all things in Scripture are equally plain or clear.
*   **Salvation is Clear:** However, those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation are so clearly propounded and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, may attain a sufficient understanding of them.
*   **Role of the Spirit:** While the text is clear, the Confession acknowledges that the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit is necessary for the saving understanding of Scripture.

### 5. The Sufficiency of Scripture (Chapter 1, Section 6)
*   The whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture.
*   Nothing is to be added to Scripture, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or traditions of men.

### 6. Interpretation of Scripture (Chapter 1, Section 9–10)
*   **Scripture Interprets Scripture:** The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself. Therefore, when a question arises about the true and full sense of any Scripture, it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly.
*   **The Spirit:** The Supreme Judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined is the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.
*   **The Church:** The Church is not the judge of Scripture; rather, Scripture is the judge of the Church.

### 7. Accessibility and Translation (Chapter 1, Section 8)
*   **Vernacular:** The Old Testament in Hebrew and the New Testament in Greek were originally written in the languages of the people.
*   **Translation:** These languages are now translated into the vulgar (common) languages of all people. This is done so that the Word of God may dwell in them abundantly, and all may worship God in an acceptable manner and understand His will.

### 8. The Purpose of Scripture (Chapter 1, Section 11)
*   The ultimate purpose of the Scriptures is the glory of God.
*   It is given so that man may have a full knowledge of God, His will, and the way of salvation.
*   It is to be used for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness.

### Summary
In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that the Bible is the **final, sufficient, clear, and authoritative Word of God**. It rejects any tradition or revelation that contradicts or adds to it, insists on its translation into common languages, and places it above the authority of the Church or any human council.

This high view of Scripture serves as the foundation for the rest of the Confession, which deals with God, man, salvation, the church, and the end times.

This chapter is heavily influenced by the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and the Savoy Declaration (1658), reflecting the shared Reformed theology of the time. It presents a high view of God's sovereignty, majesty, and triune nature.

Here is a breakdown of what the Confession teaches regarding God and the Trinity:

The Confession begins by establishing strict monotheism. It teaches that there is only **one living and true God**.

*   **Omnipotence and Omniscience:** He is all-powerful and all-knowing.
*   **Omnipresence:** He is present everywhere.
*   **Incomprehensibility:** While God has revealed Himself, His full essence remains beyond human understanding.

### 2. The Moral Attributes of God
The Confession emphasizes that God is not only powerful but morally perfect.
*   **Holiness and Justice:** God is "most holy" and "most just." He is "terrible in his judgments" against sin.
*   **Love and Mercy:** He is "most loving, gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness and truth."
*   **Forgiveness:** He is a forgiver of iniquity, transgression, and sin, yet He by no means clears the guilty (2.3).
*   **Truth:** He is the "faithful God" who cannot lie.

### 3. The Doctrine of the Trinity (Section 9)
The most specific teaching on the Trinity is found in **Section 9**

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** teaches a high view of God's sovereignty regarding His decree. This doctrine is primarily outlined in **Chapter 3: Of God's Decree**, though it interacts closely with Chapter 5 (Providence) and Chapter 9 (Of Free Will).

The Confession is distinctly Reformed (Calvinistic) in its soteriology. Here is a breakdown of its specific teachings on God's decree:

### 1. The Nature of the Decree
*   **Eternal and Unchangeable:** The Confession teaches that God, from all eternity, did, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass (3.1).
*   **Purpose:** The ultimate end of this decree is the manifestation of His own glory.
*   **Certainty:** Because the decree is based on God's will, nothing happens by chance or fortune. All events are certain to occur because God has ordained them.

### 2. God and Sin
*   **Not the Author of Sin:** While God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, the Confession explicitly states that God is **not** the author of sin, nor does He violate the will of the creature (3.1).
*   **Permission:** God permits sin to occur without being tainted by it. He does not force creatures to sin, but He sovereignly allows it to happen within His plan.
*   **Second Causes:** The decree does not negate secondary causes. Things happen according to their nature (e.g., fire burns, humans choose), but God's decree ensures the ultimate outcome aligns with His purpose.

### 3. Predestination (Election and Reprobation)
The Confession teaches "double predestination," meaning God has eternally decreed the destiny of both the saved and the lost.

*   **Election:** Some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life (3.3). This is not based on any foreseen faith, good works, or perseverance in the creature. It is solely based on God's "good pleasure" and sovereign will (3.5).
*   **Reprobation:** Others are foreordained to everlasting death (3.3). This is done to manifest God's justice.
*   **In Christ:** The Confession emphasizes that the elect are chosen **in Christ** before the foundation of the world (3.5). Salvation is not abstract; it is specifically tied to union with Jesus Christ.
*   **Definite Number:** The number of the elect is so certain and definite that it cannot be either increased or diminished (3.4).

### 4. The Relationship with Human Will
The Confession rejects the idea that God's decree forces people to act against their nature.
*   **Compatibilism:** God's decree is compatible with human freedom. God ordains the *actions* of free agents, but He does so in a way that preserves their voluntary nature.
*   **No Compulsion:** In the case of good works, God works in the believer to will and to do. In the case of sin, God permits the will to act according to its own corrupt nature (3.1 & 9.1).

### 5. Pastoral Application
The Confession concludes Chapter 3 with a warning on how this doctrine should be handled (3.6). It is not meant to be a subject of idle speculation or pride, but rather:
*   **Humility:** To humble the believer, recognizing salvation is entirely of grace.
*   **Assurance:** To give comfort to the elect, knowing their salvation rests on God's unchangeable purpose, not their own fluctuating performance.
*   **Praise:** To lead to the praise of God's glorious grace.
*   **Caution:** It warns that those who are not elected may not be able to understand this doctrine and may be led into despair or presumption if not taught with "special prudence and care."

### Summary Comparison
The 1689 Confession on this topic is nearly identical to **Chapter 3 of the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)**. The primary difference between the 1689 Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession lies in ecclesiology (church government) and baptism, not in the doctrine of God's decree.

**In short:** The 1689 Confession teaches that God is absolutely sovereign over all history, that He chose specific individuals for salvation solely based on His grace (not their merit), that He passed over others to demonstrate justice, and that He is in no way the author of sin despite ordaining all things.

questions.reference_answer: God the good Creator of all things, in his infinite power, and wisdom, doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all Creatures, and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence, to the end for the which they were Created; according unto his infallible foreknowledge, and the free and immutable Councel of his own will; to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, infinite goodness and mercy. Although in relation to the foreknowledge and Decree of God, the first cause, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly; so that there is not any thing, befalls any by chance, or without his Providence; yet by the same Providence he ordereth them to fall out, according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently. God in his ordinary Providence maketh use of means; yet is free to work, without, above, and against them at his pleasure. The Almighty power, unsearchable wisdom, and infinite goodness of God, so far manifest themselves in his Providence, that his determinate Councel extendeth it self even to the first fall, and all other sinful actions both of Angels, and Men; (and that not by a bare permission) which also he most wisely and powerfully boundeth, and otherwise ordereth, and governeth, in a manifold dispensation to his most holy ends: yet so, as the sinfulness of their acts proceedeth only from the Creatures, and not from God; who being most holy and righteous, neither is nor can be, the author or approver of sin. The most wise, righteous, and gracious God, doth oftentimes, leave for a season his own children to manifold temptations, and the corruptions of their own heart, to chastise them for their former sins, or to discover unto them the hidden strength of corruption, and deceitfulness of their hearts, that they may be humbled; and to raise them to a more close, and constant dependence for their support, upon himself; and to make them more watchful against all future occasions of sin, and for other just and holy ends. As for those wicked and ungodly men, whom God as a righteous judge, for former sin doth blind and harden; from them he not only withholdeth his Grace, whereby they might have been inlightned in their understanding, and wrought upon in their hearts: But sometimes also withdraweth the gifts which they had, and exposeth them to such objects as their corruptions makes occasion of sin; and withall gives them over to their own lusts, the temptations of the world, and the power of Satan, whereby it comes to pass, that they harden themselves, even under those means which God useth for the softning of others. As the Providence of God doth in general reach to all Creatures, so after a most special manner it taketh care of his Church, and disposeth of all things to the good thereof.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** addresses the doctrine of divine providence in **Chapter 5: "Of Providence."**

The Confession is a Reformed (Calvinistic) document, and its teaching on providence is nearly identical to Chapter 5 of the Westminster Confession of Faith. It presents a high view of God's sovereignty, asserting that God actively governs all events in the universe while maintaining His holiness regarding sin.

Here is a breakdown of what the 1689 Confession teaches about divine providence, organized by its key theological themes:

### 1. God’s Universal Governance (Article 1)
The Confession teaches that God, the great Creator, upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures, actions, and things.
*   **No Chance:** Nothing happens by "fortune" or "chance." Every event, from the movement of stars to the thoughts of men, falls under God's sovereign control.
*   **Preservation:** God does not merely create the universe and step away; He actively preserves it moment by moment.

### 2. God’s Decree and Foreknowledge (Article 2)
This article addresses the relationship between God's eternal plan and what happens in time.
*   **Ordained to Come to Pass:** God has foreordained whatsoever comes to pass. This means His will is the ultimate cause of all events.
*   **Not the Author of Sin:** Crucially, the Confession asserts that while God ordains events, He is **not** the author of sin. He does not commit violence, nor is He tempted by evil.
*   **Human Responsibility:** God's decree does not take away the liberty or contingency of second causes (human choices). Humans act freely and are responsible for their actions, even though those actions fulfill God's plan.

### 3. The Problem of Evil and Sin (Article 3)
The Confession tackles the difficult question of how a good God allows evil.
*   **Permission:** God permits sin to happen. He does not force people to sin, but He allows them to follow their own corrupt desires.
*   **Direction:** Even though God permits sin, He directs it to His own glory. The Confession uses the example of Joseph (Genesis 50:20), where the brothers meant evil, but God meant it for good.
*   **Limitation:** God sets boundaries on sin; He limits how far evil can go and ensures it ultimately serves His purposes.

### 4. Special vs. General Providence (Articles 4 & 5)
The Confession distinguishes between how God treats the wicked and how He treats His people.
*   **General Providence:** God sustains all creation, including the wicked.
*   **Withholding Grace:** In Article 4, it teaches that God sometimes withdraws His common grace from the wicked, leaving them to their own lusts and the corruption of their own hearts. This is a form of judgment.
*   **Special Providence:** For the elect (believers), God exercises a special providence. He preserves them through trials, guides their steps, and works all things together for their good (Romans 8:28).

### 5. Affliction and Testing (Article 7)
The Confession addresses why good people suffer.
*   **Sanctification:** God allows His children to face affliction and temptation.
*   **Purpose:** These trials are not punishments for condemnation but are designed to humble them, test their faith, and increase their dependence on God.

### 6. The Role of Means and Prayer (Articles 8 & 9)
A common objection to providence is, "If God controls everything, why pray or take action?" The Confession answers this directly.
*   **Prayer:** The duty of prayer is not abolished by God's sovereignty. Prayer is a "means" ordained by God to accomplish His ends. We pray *because* God commands it, not to change His mind, but to align ourselves with His will.
*   **Secondary Causes:** God usually works through "means" (natural laws, human effort, medicine, etc.). However, He is not bound by them. He can work without means (miracles) or contrary to means, but He typically works through them.

### Summary of Theological Implications
Based on Chapter 5, the 1689 Confession teaches a **Compatibilist** view of providence:
1.  **Sovereignty:** God is absolutely in control of history.
2.  **Responsibility:** Humans are morally responsible for their choices.
3.  **Holiness:** God is never tainted by the evil He permits.
4.  **Comfort:** Believers can trust that no tragedy is outside of God's care or ultimate plan for their good.

In short, the 1689 Confession teaches that Providence is the active, wise, and holy hand of God guiding all creation toward the ends He has eternally decreed, ensuring that His glory is displayed in both mercy and justice.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about god's covenant?
questions.reference_answer: The distance between God and the Creature is so great, that although reasonable Creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have attained the reward of Life, but by some voluntary condescension on Gods part, which he hath been pleased to express, by way of Covenant. Moreover Man having brought himself under the curse of the Law by his fall, it pleased the Lord to make a Covenant of Grace wherein he freely offereth unto Sinners, Life and Salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them Faith in him, that they may be saved; and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal Life, his holy Spirit, to make them willing, and able to believe. This Covenant is revealed in the Gospel; first of all to Adam in the promise of Salvation by the seed of the woman, and afterwards by farther steps, untill the full discovery thereof was compleated in the new Testament; and it is founded in that Eternal Covenant transaction, that was between the Father and the Son, about the Redemption of the Elect; and it is alone by the Grace of this Covenant, that all of the posterity of fallen Adam, that ever were saved, did obtain life and a blessed immortality; Man being now utterly uncapable of acceptance with God upon those terms, on which Adam stood in his state of innocency.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Chapter 7 (Of God's Covenant). Should align with the 1689 London Baptist Confession's Reformed Baptist theology.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (often called the Second London Confession) is the primary doctrinal standard for Reformed (Particular) Baptists. Its teaching on God's covenant is deeply rooted in **Covenant Theology**, sharing much in common with the Presbyterian Westminster Confession of Faith, but with distinct Baptist applications regarding the administration of the covenant and the sign of baptism.

Here is a breakdown of what the 1689 Confession teaches about God's covenant, primarily based on **Chapter 7 (Of God's Covenant)** and related chapters.

### 1. The Covenant of Works
The Confession affirms that God established a specific covenant with Adam before the Fall.
*   **The Parties:** God and Adam (as the federal head of humanity).
*   **The Condition:** Perfect, personal obedience to God's law.
*   **The Promise:** Life (eternal life in communion with God).
*   **The Penalty:** Death (spiritual and physical) if the command was broken.
*   **The Result:** Adam broke this covenant, bringing sin, guilt, and death upon all his descendants (Chapter 7.2).
*   **Significance:** This establishes that humanity cannot be saved by works, as the Covenant of Works is now broken and cannot be fulfilled by fallen man.

### 2. The Covenant of Grace
Because humanity failed in the Covenant of Works, God established a second covenant to save the elect.
*   **The Parties:** God and the Elect (represented by Christ).
*   **The Mediator:** Jesus Christ is the sole mediator of this covenant. He acts as the "Second Adam" to fulfill the obedience required and pay the penalty for sin (Chapter 7.3).
*   **The Condition:** Faith in Jesus Christ. Salvation is received through faith, not by works of the law.
*   **The Promise:** Eternal life and reconciliation with God.
*   **The Scope:** This covenant is made specifically with the elect, whom God chose in Christ before the foundation of the world (Chapter 7.3 & 8.1).

### 3. The Unity of the Covenant of Grace
A central tenet of the 1689 Confession is that there is essentially **one Covenant of Grace** throughout history, despite different administrations.
*   **Substance:** The Confession states that the Covenant of Grace is "not varied" in substance between the Old and New Testaments. The promise of salvation through the Messiah is the same in both eras (Chapter 7.6).
*   **Administration:** While the substance is the same, the *administration* differs.
    *   **Old Testament:** Administered through types, shadows, sacrifices, and prophecies pointing forward to Christ.
    *   **New Testament:** Administered through the preaching of the Word and the sacraments, with Christ having already come.
*   **Continuity:** This teaches that Old Testament saints were saved in the same way as New Testament saints: by grace through faith in the promised Messiah.

### 4. The Covenant of Redemption (Pactum Salutis)
While not explicitly titled as such in Chapter 7, the Confession teaches the concept of the Covenant of Redemption in **Chapter 8 (Of Christ the Mediator)**.
*   It teaches that before the foundation of the world, the Father and the Son entered into an eternal agreement.
*   The Father gave a people to the Son; the Son agreed to redeem them; and the Spirit agreed to apply that redemption.
*   This eternal pact is the foundation of the historical Covenant of Grace.

### 5. Baptist Distinctives: Administration and Signs
While the 1689 Confession aligns closely with Presbyterian theology on the *nature* of the covenants, it diverges on the *application* of the covenant sign, which is the primary Baptist distinctive.

*   **The Sign of the Covenant:**
    *   **Old Testament:** Circumcision was the sign and seal of the Covenant of Grace (Chapter 7.5).
    *   **New Testament:** Baptism is the sign and seal of the Covenant of Grace (Chapter 29.1).
*   **Who Receives the Sign:**
    *   Unlike the Westminster Confession (which allows for infant baptism based on the continuity of the covenant community), the 1689 Confession teaches that the sign of baptism is to be administered only to those who **profess repentance and faith** (Chapter 29.4).
    *   **Theological Implication:** Reformed Baptists interpret the "Covenant of Grace" in the New Testament as being administered strictly to believers. Therefore, the "visible church" consists of believers and their children are not automatically included in the covenant sign (baptism) unless they personally profess faith. This is often referred to as "Covenant Theology with a Baptist Ecclesiology."
*   **The Law:**
    *   The Confession teaches that the Moral Law (the Ten Commandments) continues to bind believers as a rule of life, but it is no longer a Covenant of Works (Chapter 19). Believers are not under the law as a covenant of life, but are under the law of Christ.

### Summary
The 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches a **Reformed Covenant Theology** that emphasizes:
1.  **Two Primary Covenants:** The broken Covenant of Works (Adam) and the saving Covenant of Grace (Christ).
2.  **One Saving Plan:** The Covenant of Grace is unified across history, with salvation always by grace through faith in Christ.
3.  **Christocentric:** Jesus Christ is the head and mediator of the covenant; no one is saved apart from Him.
4.  **Believer's Covenant:** While the covenant is one in substance, the New Testament administration restricts the covenant sign (baptism) to those who personally profess faith, distinguishing the visible church from the nation of Israel.

This framework allows Reformed Baptists to affirm the sovereignty of God in salvation (like Presbyterians) while maintaining the practice of Believer's Baptism (unlike Presbyterians).

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God in his eternal purpose, to chuse and ordain the Lord Jesus his only begotten Son, according to the Covenant made between them both, to be the Mediator between God and Man; the Prophet, Priest and King; Head and Saviour of his Church, the heir of all things, and judge of the world: Unto whom he did from all Eternity give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second Person in the Holy Trinity, being very and eternal God, the brightness of the Fathers glory, of one substance and equal with him: who made the World, who upholdeth and governeth all things he hath made: did when the fullness of time was come take unto him mans nature, with all the Essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the Womb of the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit coming down upon her, and the power of the most High overshadowing her, and so was made of a Woman, of the Tribe of Judah, of the Seed of Abraham, and David according to the Scriptures: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, were inseparably joined together in one Person: without conversion, composition, or confusion: which Person is very God, and very Man; yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and Man. The Lord Jesus in his humane nature thus united to the divine, in the Person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell: To the end that being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of Grace, and Truth, he might be throughly furnished to execute the office of a Mediator, and Surety; which office he took not upon himself, but was thereunto called by his Father; who also put all power and judgement in his hand, and gave him Commandement to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which that he might discharge he was made under the Law, and did perfectly fulfill it, and underwent the punishment due to us, which we should have born and suffered, being made Sin and a Curse for us: enduring most grievous sorrows in his Soul; and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died, and remained in the state of the dead; yet saw no corruption: on the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which he also ascended into heaven: and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge Men and Angels, at the end of the World. The Lord Jesus by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the Eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the Justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an Everlasting inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the price of Redemption was not actually paid by Christ, till after his Incarnation, yet the vertue, efficacy, and benefit thereof were communicated to the Elect in all ages successively, from the beginning of the World, in and by those Promises, Types, and Sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the Seed of the Woman, which should bruise the Serpents head; and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the World: Being the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Christ in the work of Mediation acteth according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to it self; yet by reason of the Unity of the Person, that which is proper to one nature, is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the Person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, he doth certainly, and effectually apply, and communicate the same; making intercession for them, uniting them to himself by his spirit, revealing unto them, in and by the word, the mystery of salvation; perswading them to believe, and obey; governing their hearts by his word and spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his Almighty power, and wisdom; in such manner, and wayes as are most consonant to his wonderful, and unsearchable dispensation; and all of free, and absolute Grace, without any condition foreseen in them, to procure it. This office of Mediator between God and Man, is proper onely to Christ, who is the Prophet, Priest, and King of the Church of God; and may not be either in whole, or any part thereof transfer'd from him to any other. This number and order of Offices is necessary; for in respect of our ignorance, we stand in need of his prophetical Office; and in respect of our alienation from God, and imperfection of the best of our services, we need his Priestly office, to reconcile us, and present us acceptable unto God: and in respect our averseness, and utter inability to return to God, and for our rescue, and security from our spiritual adversaries, we need his Kingly office, to convince, subdue, draw, uphold, deliver, and preserve us to his Heavenly Kingdome.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (LBCF) addresses the doctrine of Christ the Mediator primarily in **Chapter 8: "Of Christ the Mediator."**

This chapter is heavily influenced by the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) but reflects the distinct theological commitments of the Particular (Reformed) Baptists. It outlines the person, work, and ongoing ministry of Jesus Christ as the sole bridge between a holy God and sinful humanity.

Here is a breakdown of what the 1689 Confession teaches about Christ the Mediator, organized by key theological themes:

### 1. The Person of the Mediator (The Hypostatic Union)
The Confession begins by establishing that the Mediator must be both fully God and fully man to effectively reconcile the two parties.
*   **Divine and Human:** The Lord Jesus, the eternal Son of God, took upon Himself human nature. He possesses "two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, that is to say, the Godhead and the Manhood, which were never divided."
*   **One Person:** These two natures are united in one person ("without conversion, composition, or confusion").
*   **True God and True Man:** He is "very God and very man," yet one Christ, the only Mediator.
*   **Sinlessness:** He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. While He took on human nature, He was "without sin," making Him a suitable sacrifice.

### 2. The Appointment to the Office
The Confession teaches that Christ's mediation was not an afterthought but part of God's eternal decree.
*   **Divine Appointment:** God the Father appointed the Son to be the Mediator between God and man.
*   **The Covenant:** This appointment is rooted in the Covenant of Grace. The Father gave a people to the Son to be redeemed, and the Son agreed to become their surety and mediator.

### 3. The Work of the Mediator (Obedience and Atonement)
The Confession details the specific actions Christ undertook to fulfill His mediatorial office.
*   **Perfect Obedience:** Christ perfectly fulfilled the moral law of God. He lived a life of perfect righteousness on behalf of His people (Active Obedience).
*   **Sacrificial Death:** He offered Himself as a sacrifice to satisfy divine justice. He bore the sins of His people and endured the wrath of God (Passive Obedience).
*   **Resurrection and Ascension:** He rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, and now sits at the right hand of the Father. This confirms the acceptance of His sacrifice and His authority.

### 4. The Ongoing Ministry of the Mediator (Intercession)
The mediation of Christ is not limited to His earthly life; it continues in heaven.
*   **Heavenly Intercession:** Christ continually makes intercession for His people. He presents His sacrifice before the Father and pleads their cause.
*   **Preservation:** Through His intercession, He secures the salvation of His elect, ensuring that they are kept by the power of God through faith.
*   **Judgment:** He is appointed to judge the world at the last day.

### 5. The Exclusivity of the Mediator
A crucial point in the Confession is the exclusivity of Christ's mediation.
*   **No Other Mediator:** The Confession explicitly states that there is no other mediator between God and man but Christ alone.
*   **Rejection of Saints and Priests:** It rejects the idea that saints, angels, or a human priesthood can act as mediators. Believers are to pray directly to God in the name of Christ, not through the intercession of Mary or the saints.
*   **Sufficiency:** Christ's mediation is sufficient for all who come to God through Him; nothing needs to be added to His work.

### 6. The Imputation of Christ's Righteousness
While closely related to Chapter 11 (Justification), Chapter 8 establishes the basis for this doctrine.
*   **Imputed Obedience:** The obedience and satisfaction of Christ are accepted by God in the place of the sinner.
*   **Justification:** Believers are justified not by their own works, but by the mediation of Christ, whose righteousness is imputed to them.

### Summary
In the 1689 London Baptist Confession, **Christ the Mediator** is the central figure of redemption. He is the **God-Man** who bridges the infinite gap caused by sin. Through His **perfect life, atoning death, and heavenly intercession**, He secures salvation for the elect. The Confession emphasizes that this work is **complete, exclusive, and sufficient**, requiring no human addition or priestly intercession to be effective.

***

**Key Quote from Chapter 8, Section 1:**
> *"The Lord Jesus, in his human nature thus united to the divine, in the person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure, having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell; to the end that, being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of grace and truth, he might be thoroughly furnished to execute the office of a mediator, and surety."*

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about effectual calling?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God hath predestinated unto Life, he is pleased in his appointed, and accepted time, effectually to call by his word, and Spirit, out of that state of sin, and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and Salvation by Jesus Christ; inlightning their minds, spiritually, and savingly to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his Almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his Grace. This Effectual Call is of God's free, and special grace alone, not from any thing at all foreseen in man, nor from any power, or agency in the Creature, coworking with his special Grace, the Creature being wholly passive therein, being dead in sins and trespasses, until being quickned & renewed by the holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the Grace offered and conveyed in it; and that by no less power, then that which raised up Christ from the dead. Elect Infants dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit; who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth: so also are all other elect persons, who are uncapable of being outwardly called by the Ministry of the Word. Others not elected, although they may be called by the Ministry of the word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet not being effectually drawn by the Father, they neither will, nor can truly come to Christ; and therefore cannot be saved: much less can men that receive not the Christian Religion be saved; be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, and the Law of that Religion they do profess.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the Second London Confession) addresses the doctrine of effectual calling in **Chapter 10**.

This chapter outlines the Reformed Baptist understanding of how God saves individuals, emphasizing that salvation is entirely the work of God's sovereign grace, applied to the elect through the Holy Spirit.

Here is a breakdown of what the Confession teaches regarding effectual calling, based on the three paragraphs of Chapter 10:

### 1. The Source and Nature of the Call (Paragraph 1)
The Confession teaches that effectual calling is a specific work of God directed only toward those He has chosen (the elect).
*   **Divine Initiative:** It is God who calls. Those whom God has predestined to life are "effectually called" by His Word and Spirit.
*   **The Transformation:** This calling is not merely an external invitation. It involves a supernatural internal change:
    *   **Enlightenment:** Their minds are "spiritually and savingly enlightened" to understand the things of God.
    *   **Regeneration:** The "heart of stone" is taken away and replaced with a "heart of flesh."
    *   **Renewal of Will:** Their wills are renewed and determined by God to that which is good.
*   **The Result:** They are "effectually drawn" to Jesus Christ.
*   **Human Freedom:** The Confession addresses the tension between divine sovereignty and human responsibility. It states that while God determines the will, the individual comes to Christ **"most freely,"** because their will has been made willing by God's grace.

### 2. The Distinction Between the Elect and the Non-Elect (Paragraph 2)
The Confession distinguishes between the "outward call" (the preaching of the Gospel) and the "effectual call" (saving grace).
*   **The Non-Elect:** Others who are not elected may hear the ministry of the Word and may experience "some common operations of the Spirit."
*   **No Salvation:** However, because they are not effectually called, they never truly come to Christ. Consequently, they cannot be saved.
*   **Exclusivity:** This teaches that the saving call is exclusive to the elect; it is not universal in its saving efficacy.

### 3. Special Cases: Infants and the Incapable (Paragraph 3)
The Confession acknowledges that the "outward call" (preaching) is not the only means by which the Spirit works.
*   **Elect Infants:** Those who are elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit.
*   **Incapable Persons:** The Spirit works "when, where, and how He pleases." Therefore, other elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word (due to age, mental capacity, or circumstance) are also regenerated and saved.

### Key Theological Themes
Based on Chapter 10, the 1689 Confession teaches the following core principles regarding effectual calling:

1.  **Monergism:** Salvation is the work of God alone. The human will, in its natural state, is dead in sin and cannot choose God unless God first renews it.
2.  **Irresistible Grace:** While the language "irresistible" is not used, the concept is present. God "effectually draws" the elect. The resistance of the natural will is overcome by the Spirit's power.
3.  **Particular Redemption:** The call is specific to the elect, not a general offer that depends on human acceptance for its efficacy.
4.  **Compatibilism:** The Confession maintains that God's sovereignty does not violate human freedom. The elect come to Christ willingly, but that willingness is the result of God's grace.

### Summary Quote
The essence of the teaching is captured in the first paragraph:
> *"Those whom God hath predestinated unto life, he is pleased, in his appointed and accepted time, effectually to call, by his Word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation, by Jesus Christ; enlightening their minds spiritually and savingly to understand the things of God... taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ: yet so, as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace."* (1689 LBCF, Chapter 10, Paragraph 1)

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about justification?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God Effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth, not by infusing Righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting, and accepting their Persons as Righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone, not by imputing faith it self, the act of beleiving, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their Righteousness; but by imputing Christs active obedience unto the whole Law, and passive obedience in his death, for their whole and sole Righteousnnss, they receiving, and resting on him, and his Righteousness, by Faith; which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God. Faith thus receiving and resting on Christ, and his Righteousness, is the alone instrument of Justification: yet it is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving Graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love. Christ by his obedience, and death, did fully discharge the debt of all those that are justified; and did by the sacrifice of himself, in the blood of his cross, undergoing in their stead, the penalty due unto them: make a proper, real and full satisfaction to Gods justice in their behalf: yet in asmuch as he was given by the Father for them, and his Obedience and Satisfaction accepted in their stead, and both freely, not for any thing in them; their Justification is only of Free Grace, that both the exact justice and rich Grace of God, might be glorified in the Justification of sinners. God did from all eternity decreeto justifie all the Elect, and Christ did in the fulness of time die for their sins, and rise again for their Justification; Nevertheless they are not justified personally, untill the Holy Spirit, doth in due time actually apply Christ unto them. God doth continue to Forgive the sins of those that are justified, and although they can never fall from the state of justication; yet they may by their sins fall under Gods Fatherly displeasure; and in that condition, they have not usually the light of his Countenance restored unto them, untill they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith, and repentance. The Justification of Believers under the Old Testament was in all these respects, one and the same with the justification of Believers under the New Tement.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (LBCF) addresses the doctrine of justification in **Chapter 11**. As a Reformed (Calvinistic) confession, its teaching aligns closely with the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and the Savoy Declaration (1658), but it is written from a Baptist perspective regarding church polity and covenant theology.

Here is a summary of what the 1689 Confession teaches about justification, broken down by key theological themes:

### 1. The Definition: Imputation, Not Infusion
The Confession explicitly rejects the Roman Catholic view of justification as a process of making a person internally righteous (infusion). Instead, it teaches that justification is a legal declaration.
*   **Pardon and Acceptance:** God justifies sinners by pardoning their sins and accepting their persons as righteous.
*   **Imputation:** This righteousness is not found within the sinner. Rather, God **imputes** (credits) the righteousness of Christ to the believer.
*   **Text Reference:** *"Not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous... but by imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ unto them."* (11.1)

### 2. The Ground: Christ’s Active and Passive Obedience
The Confession teaches that the sole basis for justification is the work of Jesus Christ. It specifies two aspects of Christ's work:
*   **Passive Obedience:** Christ’s suffering and death, which paid the penalty for sin (satisfaction of God's justice).
*   **Active Obedience:** Christ’s perfect life of law-keeping, which is credited to the believer.
*   **Text Reference:** The Confession states that Christ "did fully discharge the debt of all those that are thus justified, and did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to his Father's justice in their behalf." (11.3)

### 3. The Instrument: Faith Alone (*Sola Fide*)
The Confession affirms that faith is the only means by which a sinner receives justification.
*   **Instrumental, Not Meritorious:** Faith is the "instrument" that receives Christ's righteousness. It is not the *ground* of justification (Christ is the ground), nor is faith itself counted as the righteousness.
*   **Faith is a Gift:** The Confession emphasizes monergism (God working alone in salvation), stating that the faith required for justification is "the gift of God."
*   **Text Reference:** *"Faith, thus receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness, is the alone instrument of justification... which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God."* (11.1, 11.2)

### 4. The Relationship to Good Works
The 1689 Confession is careful to distinguish between the *cause* of justification and the *evidence* of justification.
*   **Not the Cause:** Justification is not based on any works done by the sinner, nor is it based on "evangelical obedience" (good works done after conversion).
*   **The Fruit:** While good works do not justify, true faith is never alone. Justification is always accompanied by sanctification. Good works are the necessary fruit and evidence of a justifying faith.
*   **Text Reference:** *"Yet is it not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love."* (11.2)

### 5. The Timing: Eternal Decree vs. Temporal Application
The Confession makes a distinction between God's eternal plan and the believer's experience in time.
*   **Eternal Decree:** God decreed to justify the elect from eternity.
*   **Temporal Application:** However, individuals are not actually justified until the Holy Spirit applies Christ to them in "due time." This prevents the error of Universalism (that everyone is justified regardless of faith) while maintaining the sovereignty of God.
*   **Text Reference:** *"God did, from all eternity, decree to justify all the elect... nevertheless, they are not justified, until the Holy Spirit doth, in due time, actually apply Christ unto them."* (11.4)

### 6. The Security of Justification
The Confession teaches that justification is a permanent state.
*   **Once for All:** Justification is not repeated. Once a person is justified, they remain in that state.
*   **No Loss:** Because it is based on Christ's finished work and God's free grace, a believer cannot lose their justification.
*   **Text Reference:** *"The Lord Jesus... hath fully satisfied the justice of his Father... for all those whom the Father hath given unto him."* (11.5)

### Summary
In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that **justification is a free act of God's grace**, wherein He pardons the sinner and counts them as righteous solely on the basis of **Christ's obedience and sacrifice**. This is received through **faith alone**, which is itself a gift from God, and results in a permanent standing before God that is evidenced by a life of good works.

This perseverance of the Saints depends not upon their own free will; but upon the immutability of the decree of Election flowing from the free and unchangeable love of God the Father; upon the efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ and Union with him, the oath of God, the abiding of his Spirit & the seed of God within them, and the nature of the Covenant of Grace from all which ariseth also the certainty and infallibility thereof. And though they may through the temptation of Satan and of the world, the prevalency of corruption remaining in them, and the neglect of means of their preservation fall into grievous sins, and for a time continue therein; whereby they incur Gods displeasure, and grieve his holy Spirit, come to have their graces and comforts impaired have their hearts hardened, and their Consciences wounded, hurt, and scandalize others, and bring temporal judgements upon themselves: yet they shall renew their repentance and be preserved through faith in Christ Jesus to the end.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** addresses the doctrine of the Perseverance of the Saints in **Chapter 17**.

The Confession teaches that true believers, those who are effectually called and regenerated by God, are eternally secure in their salvation. They cannot lose their salvation, though they may fall into sin.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the teaching based on the four sections of Chapter 17:

### 1. The Certainty of Perseverance (Section 1)
The Confession asserts that those whom God has accepted, effectually called, and sanctified by His Spirit **cannot totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace.**

*   **The Subject:** This promise applies only to those who are truly regenerated ("accepted," "effectually called," "sanctified"). It does not apply to mere professors of faith who lack true regeneration.
*   **The Guarantee:** Their preservation is not based on their own free will or strength, but on the unchangeable love of God.
*   **The Reasons:** The Confession lists five specific theological foundations for this security:
    1.  **God's Decree:** The immutability of His decree of election.
    2.  **The Covenant:** The efficacy of the covenant of grace.
    3.  **Union with Christ:** The believer's inseparable union with Christ.
    4.  **Christ's Intercession:** Christ's ongoing prayer and mediation for His people.
    5.  **The Spirit:** The indwelling presence of the Holy Spirit and the seed of God within them.

### 2. The Reality of Sin and Backsliding (Section 2)
The Confession is careful to distinguish between *losing salvation* and *falling into sin*. It teaches that perseverance does not mean sinless perfection.

*   **Falling into Sin:** True believers can fall into sin through temptations and the assaults of Satan.
*   **Consequences:** When they sin, they may be:
    *   Hardened in their hearts.
    *   Wounded in their conscience.
    *   Grieve the Holy Spirit.
    *   Temporarily deprived of some measure of God's light and comfort.
*   **Restoration:** However, they will be renewed and kept by God's power. They will not be cast off completely.

### 3. The Means of Preservation (Section 3)
The Confession emphasizes that the preservation of the saints is an act of God's power, not human effort.

*   **God's Power:** Believers are kept by the power of God through faith.
*   **Salvation:** This preservation is "unto salvation."
*   **Struggle:** While they may struggle and experience spiritual dryness or discipline, the ultimate outcome is secure.

### 4. The Result (Section 4)
The final section summarizes the outcome of this doctrine.

*   **Eternal Security:** Because of the reasons listed in Section 1, the saints will be eternally saved.
*   **Assurance:** This doctrine is intended to provide comfort and assurance to the believer, knowing that their security rests on God's faithfulness rather than their own fluctuating performance.

### Summary of Key Distinctions
The 1689 Confession makes two vital distinctions regarding this doctrine:
1.  **Temporary vs. Final:** A believer may fall away *temporarily* (in terms of fellowship, joy, or service) but not *finally* (in terms of their eternal state).
2.  **True vs. False Professors:** Those who appear to fall away completely and permanently were never truly part of the elect or regenerated in the first place (echoing 1 John 2:19).

In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches **Eternal Security**, grounded in the sovereignty of God and the finished work of Christ, while acknowledging the reality of the believer's ongoing struggle with sin.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** addresses the doctrine of the Last Judgment primarily in **Chapter 33**, titled "Of the Last Judgment." It also draws context from **Chapter 32**, "Of the State of Man after Death and of the Resurrection of the Dead."

Here is a summary of what the Confession teaches regarding the Last Judgment:

### 1. The Appointment and the Judge
The Confession teaches that God has appointed a specific day for judgment. While the exact time is unknown to men, it is certain. The Judge of this day is **Jesus Christ**, the Son of God.
*   **Text:** "God hath appointed a day, wherein he will judge the world in righteousness by Jesus Christ..." (Chapter 33, Section 1).
*   **Significance:** This affirms the deity and authority of Christ as the ultimate arbiter of human destiny.

### 2. The Scope of the Judgment
The judgment is universal in scope. It is not limited to a specific group of people or nations.
*   **Subjects:** All people (both the living and the dead) and fallen angels will stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
*   **Text:** "...in which all persons that shall appear before him, shall be judged; and the angels also shall be judged..." (Chapter 33, Section 1).

### 3. The Purpose of the Judgment
The ultimate goal of the Last Judgment is the manifestation of God's glory. Specifically, it displays two attributes of God:
*   **Mercy:** Displayed in the salvation and reward of the elect.
*   **Justice:** Displayed in the punishment of the wicked.
*   **Text:** "...to the manifestation of the glory of his mercy, in the eternal salvation of the elect; and of his justice, in the eternal damnation of the reprobate..." (Chapter 33, Section 2).

### 4. The Basis of Judgment
The Confession teaches that judgment will be rendered according to **works**. However, within Reformed theology, this is understood not as salvation *by* works, but works as the necessary evidence of faith and the nature of the soul.
*   **Secret Things:** The judgment will expose all secret things, including the motives of the heart and hidden sins. Nothing will remain hidden.
*   **Text:** "...according to their works, whether good or evil... and also the secrets of all hearts..." (Chapter 33, Section 3).

### 5. The Eternal Destinies
The Confession outlines two distinct, eternal outcomes for humanity:
*   **The Wicked:** Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel will be cast into **eternal punishment** (hell), separated from the presence of God.
*   **The Righteous:** Those who are justified by faith will enter into **eternal life**, enjoying the presence and glory of God.
*   **Text:** "...the wicked, who know not God, and obey not the gospel of Jesus Christ, shall be cast into eternal torments... and the righteous... shall be received into eternal life..." (Chapter 33, Section 4).

### 6. The Practical Purpose for Believers
The Confession concludes by explaining why this doctrine is taught. It is not merely for speculation but for practical spiritual application:
*   **Holiness:** To encourage believers to pursue holiness and godliness.
*   **Comfort:** To comfort the afflicted who suffer for righteousness.
*   **Warning:** To warn the wicked of the coming wrath.
*   **Text:** "...that the doctrine of the last judgment... may be a motive to holiness... and a comfort to the afflicted..." (Chapter 33, Section 5).

### Summary
In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that the Last Judgment is a future, certain event presided over by Jesus Christ. It will be a public, universal declaration of God's justice and mercy, where every human and angel will be judged based on their works and the secrets of their hearts, resulting in either eternal life or eternal punishment. This doctrine serves to motivate believers toward holiness and comfort them in suffering.

questions.response:
The question of whether "fallen man" (humanity after the Fall of Adam and Eve) is able to choose God of his own free will is one of the most significant and debated topics in Christian theology. There is no single, universally agreed-upon answer; rather, the answer depends entirely on which theological tradition or denomination one asks.

Here is a breakdown of the major perspectives on this issue:

### 1. The Reformed / Calvinist Perspective (Monergism)
**Answer:** No, not without divine intervention.
*   **Key Doctrine:** **Total Depravity.** This does not mean humans are as evil as possible, but that sin affects every part of a person (mind, will, emotions). Spiritually, fallen man is "dead" in sin (Ephesians 2:1).
*   **The Will:** The will is in **bondage** to sin. A person can choose what they desire, but because their nature is corrupted, they naturally desire sin and cannot desire God.
*   **The Mechanism:** Salvation is **monergistic** (worked by one agent). God must first regenerate (give new spiritual life to) the sinner. Only *after* God changes the heart can the person choose to believe.
*   **Key Scripture:** *"No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him"* (John 6:44); *"The mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God; it does not submit to God's law, nor can it do so"* (Romans 8:7).

### 2. The Arminian / Wesleyan Perspective (Synergism)
**Answer:** Yes, enabled by grace.
*   **Key Doctrine:** **Prevenient Grace.** While humans are fallen and cannot save themselves, God extends a grace to *all* people that counteracts the effects of sin just enough to restore moral ability.
*   **The Will:** This grace restores the freedom of the will regarding spiritual matters. It does not force salvation, but it enables the person to accept or reject it.
*   **The Mechanism:** Salvation is **synergistic** (worked by two agents cooperating). God provides the grace and the opportunity, but the human must exercise their free will to accept it.
*   **Key Scripture:** *"The true light that gives light to everyone was coming into the world"* (John 1:9); *"Look, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in"* (Revelation 3:20).

### 3. The Roman Catholic Perspective
**Answer:** Yes, through cooperation with grace.
*   **Key Doctrine:** **Grace and Free Will.** Catholic theology teaches that Original Sin wounded human nature but did not destroy it. Humans retain free will, though it is weakened.
*   **The Will:** God's grace is necessary for salvation, but it does not override human freedom. Grace invites and empowers, but the human must cooperate (say "yes") to that grace.
*   **The Mechanism:** This is a form of **synergism**. Justification is a process involving faith and works (cooperation with grace), initiated by God but requiring human consent.
*   **Key Concept:** The Council of Trent condemned the idea that man is entirely passive in salvation, affirming that man can resist grace.

### 4. The Eastern Orthodox Perspective
**Answer:** Yes, through synergy (cooperation).
*   **Key Doctrine:** **Theosis.** Salvation is viewed as healing and union with God rather than just a legal transaction.
*   **The Will:** Humanity is viewed as having a "wounded" nature rather than a "totally depraved" one. Humans are capable of responding to God, but they cannot achieve salvation without God's energy.
*   **The Mechanism:** Salvation is a **synergy** between God's grace and human freedom. God initiates, but man must actively participate in the process of becoming holy.

### 5. The Lutheran Perspective
**Answer:** No, regarding salvation (Bondage of the Will).
*   **Key Doctrine:** Martin Luther famously wrote *The Bondage of the Will*, arguing that in spiritual matters, the will is enslaved to sin.
*   **The Will:** Like the Reformed tradition, Lutherans believe man cannot choose God on his own. However, Lutherans generally differ from Calvinists on the extent of predestination.
*   **The Mechanism:** The Holy Spirit works through the Word and Sacraments to create faith. The will is passive in conversion (like a stone being carved), but active in the life of the believer afterward.

### Summary of the Tension
The debate essentially centers on two biblical truths that seem to contradict one another:
1.  **God's Sovereignty:** Scripture says God chooses us, draws us, and gives us faith.
2.  **Human Responsibility:** Scripture commands all people to repent and believe, implying they have the ability to do so.

*   **Calvinists** prioritize the first, arguing that if man could choose God, salvation would be by works.
*   **Arminians/Catholics** prioritize the second, arguing that if man cannot choose God, God is unjust in commanding repentance or punishing unbelief.

### Conclusion
If you ask a **Calvinist**, the answer is **no**; God must change the heart first.
If you ask an **Arminian, Catholic, or Orthodox Christian**, the answer is **yes**; God provides the grace necessary to enable the choice, but the individual must make the choice.

Most theologians agree on one thing: **Without God's grace, no one chooses God.** The disagreement lies in *how* that grace interacts with human will (whether it restores the ability to choose or creates the choice itself).

questions.response:
The answer to this question depends heavily on which theological tradition is being consulted, as Christian theology holds different views on the extent of human depravity and the nature of grace. However, the term "unregenerate" is most commonly associated with **Reformed (Calvinist)** theology.

Here is a breakdown of the answer based on the major theological perspectives, with a focus on the Reformed view, which provides the most rigorous definition of the terms used.

### 1. The Reformed / Calvinist Perspective
In Reformed theology, the answer is generally **no**, with a specific distinction made between *civil good* and *spiritual good*.

*   **Total Depravity:** This doctrine teaches that sin affects every part of a person (mind, will, emotions). An unregenerate person is "spiritually dead" (Ephesians 2:1). Because they are dead, they cannot initiate spiritual life or please God on their own.
*   **The Motive Matters:** While an unregenerate person can perform actions that are morally good by human standards (e.g., feeding the poor, telling the truth, building a hospital), these actions are not considered "spiritually good" in God's sight because they are not done **in faith** and **for the glory of God**.
*   **Key Scripture:**
    *   **Romans 8:7–8:** "The mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God; it does not submit to God's law, nor can it do so. Those who are in the realm of the flesh cannot please God."
    *   **Hebrews 11:6:** "And without faith it is impossible to please God..."
    *   **Isaiah 64:6:** "All of us have become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags..."
*   **Civil Righteousness:** Reformed theologians (like John Calvin) acknowledge that unbelievers can perform "civil righteousness." They can maintain order in society and act kindly toward neighbors. However, these acts do not merit salvation, nor do they make the person acceptable to God in a spiritual sense.

### 2. The Lutheran Perspective
Martin Luther held a view very similar to the Reformed regarding salvation. He distinguished between **two kinds of righteousness**:
*   **Civil Righteousness:** Unbelievers can do good works that benefit society.
*   **Spiritual Righteousness:** Only a believer, justified by faith, can do works that are pleasing to God.
Luther famously argued that even the best works of an unbeliever are sinful because they are not done out of faith in Christ.

### 3. The Arminian / Wesleyan Perspective
Arminian theology emphasizes **Prevenient Grace**.
*   **Prevenient Grace:** This is the belief that God's grace goes before a person, restoring a measure of free will to all humans, even before they are converted.
*   **The Answer:** Because of this grace, an unregenerate person *can* choose to do good and respond to God's drawing. However, for a work to be truly "spiritually good" (meritorious for salvation), it must eventually be accompanied by saving faith. Without faith, the works cannot save, but the capacity to do good is not entirely extinguished until regeneration occurs.

### 4. The Roman Catholic Perspective
Catholic theology distinguishes between **natural good** and **supernatural good**.
*   **Natural Good:** An unregenerate (unbaptized) person can do good works based on natural law and reason. These are morally good and beneficial to society.
*   **Supernatural Good:** To do a work that is meritorious for eternal life (spiritually good in the highest sense), one must be in a state of **sanctifying grace** (usually through baptism). Without this grace, good works cannot merit salvation, though they are still considered "good" in a moral sense.

### 5. The "Cornelius" Nuance (Acts 10)
A common challenge to the "No" answer is the story of Cornelius in Acts 10. He was a devout man who prayed and gave to the poor *before* Peter preached the Gospel to him.
*   **Reformed Interpretation:** Cornelius was likely already elect and possessed saving faith (perhaps implicit) before Peter arrived. His works were evidence of the grace already at work in him, not the cause of his acceptance.
*   **Other Interpretations:** Some argue this shows that God accepts sincere seekers who have not yet heard the full Gospel, though they still require Christ for salvation.

### Summary
If you are asking from a **strictly Reformed/Protestant** standpoint (which typically uses the term "unregenerate"):
*   **Can they do good things?** Yes (Civil righteousness).
*   **Can they do anything spiritually good in God's sight?** No. Without faith and regeneration, their works lack the proper motive (glory to God) and the proper foundation (union with Christ), and therefore cannot please God or merit salvation.

If you are asking from a **broader Christian** standpoint:
*   Most traditions agree that while unbelievers can do **moral** good that benefits humanity, **spiritual** good (works that please God for the purpose of salvation) requires the work of the Holy Spirit and faith in Christ.

***Disclaimer:** I am an AI, not a theologian. This summary reflects historical Christian doctrines. For specific spiritual guidance, consulting a pastor or theologian within your specific tradition is recommended.*

However, within the framework of **historic Christian theology**, the overwhelming consensus is **yes**: the Fall (the disobedience of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3) affected every part of human nature.

This doctrine is often referred to as **Total Depravity** (in Reformed theology) or the **wounding of human nature** (in Catholic and Orthodox theology).

Here is a breakdown of how different traditions understand the scope of the Fall's effect on human nature.

### 1. The Scope of the Corruption
Most orthodox Christian traditions agree that the Fall was not merely a legal transaction but an ontological change that permeated the whole person.

*   **The Intellect (Mind):** Human reason is no longer neutral. While humans can still do science, math, and philosophy, the mind is prone to spiritual blindness. Augustine argued that the intellect is darkened regarding spiritual truths, making it difficult to know God without divine revelation.
*   **The Will:** This is the most debated area. The traditional view is that the human will is in "bondage." Humans still make choices, but their desires are naturally inclined toward self rather than God. They cannot choose spiritual good (salvation) without the intervention of grace.
*   **The Emotions (Desires):** Desires are disordered. Love is often turned inward (self-love) rather than outward (love of God and neighbor). Passions are prone to excess or deficiency.
*   **The Body:** The Fall introduced physical mortality, suffering, and decay. The body is no longer in perfect harmony with the soul; it is subject to disease and death.
*   **Relationships:** The Fall fractured relationships vertically (with God) and horizontally (with other humans and creation). This is seen in the immediate aftermath of the Fall in Genesis: blame-shifting, shame, and violence (Cain and Abel).

### 2. Differences in Theological Traditions
While all agree the Fall affected *every part*, they disagree on the *severity* of that effect.

#### **Reformed / Calvinist View (Total Depravity)**
*   **The View:** Every faculty of human nature is corrupted by sin.
*   **Nuance:** "Total" does not mean humans are as evil as they could possibly be (total depravity does not mean total depravity of *capacity*). It means the *extent* of sin reaches every part of the person.
*   **Imago Dei (Image of God):** The Image of God is marred and distorted but not erased. Humans retain dignity and rationality, but they cannot use these faculties to save themselves.

#### **Roman Catholic View (Wounded Nature)**
*   **The View:** Original Sin wounded human nature but did not destroy it.
*   **Nuance:** Reason and free will remain intact, though they are weakened. Humans can still perform "natural good" (civic virtue, charity) through natural law, but they cannot achieve "supernatural good" (salvation) without grace.
*   **Imago Dei:** The Image of God remains, but it is obscured by sin.

#### **Eastern Orthodox View (Ancestral Sin)**
*   **The View:** Humans inherit the *consequences* of the Fall (mortality and a propensity to sin) but not the *guilt* of Adam.
*   **Nuance:** Human nature is "sick" rather than "dead." The Image of God is fully intact, but it is obscured by the "passions" and death. The goal is *theosis* (restoration) rather than just legal justification.

### 3. Important Distinctions
To understand this doctrine accurately, two distinctions are necessary:

**A. Civil Good vs. Spiritual Good**
Most theologians (even those who believe in Total Depravity) acknowledge that fallen humans can still do "civil good." Unbelievers can build hospitals, write symphonies, and act justly in society. This is often attributed to **Common Grace**. However, the doctrine asserts that without grace, no human action is spiritually pleasing to God or meritorious for salvation.

**B. The Image of God (Imago Dei)**
If the Fall affected *every* part of human nature, did it destroy the Image of God?
*   **No.** Almost all Christian traditions hold that the *Imago Dei* remains. If it were destroyed, humans would cease to be human.
*   The Fall **defaced** the image (like a coin that is bent or dirty), but it did not **erase** it. This is why human life retains sacred value even after the Fall.

### 4. Alternative Views
*   **Pelagianism (Historical Heresy):** Taught that the Fall had no effect on human nature; humans are born morally neutral and can choose good or evil without divine aid. This was rejected by the early Church.
*   **Modern Secularism:** Often views human nature through an evolutionary lens. "Sin" is viewed as selfish genetic programming or social conditioning, not a spiritual Fall. In this view, human nature is flawed but perfectible through education and social reform.

### Summary
In the context of traditional Christian theology, **yes, the Fall affects every part of human nature.** It touches the mind, will, emotions, body, and relationships. However, it does not destroy human dignity or the capacity for "common good," nor does it erase the Image of God. The doctrine is usually taught not to depress humanity, but to explain the universal need for redemption.

*Disclaimer: This is a theological summary. Views may vary among specific denominations and individual believers.*
